title: There is a terrifying moment in Scripture that most people read too quickly.
paragraphs: There is a terrifying moment in Scripture that most people read too quickly.
A moment where heaven completely ignores earthly status.
A moment where positions, titles, religious reputation, influence, clothing, authority, wealth, and public honor suddenly become weightless before God.
Jesus never said, “Many will say to Me in that day, ‘Lord, did we not have important titles?’”

“Many will say to Me in that day, ‘Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy name have cast out devils? and in thy name done many wonderful works?’ And then will I profess unto them, ‘I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.’”
The Greek text is even heavier.
The phrase “I never knew you” comes from:
The Greek word γινώσκω (ginōskō) speaks of intimate relational knowing.
“I was never in covenant intimacy with you.”
That should shake every platform-driven generation alive right now.
Because modern Christianity often rewards visibility more than holiness.
Pastor. Prophet. Apostle. Evangelist. Leader. Influencer. CEO. Founder. Bishop. Doctor. Minister.
But heaven is not impressed by branding.
In Scripture, God repeatedly dismantles human obsession with status.
The Hebrew language itself exposes this.
In the Old Testament, one of the common words for glory is:
Often translated “glory,” the root idea literally carries the sense of weight.
What truly has weight before God?
Not applause. Not followers. Not religious clothing. Not public recognition.
Character carries weight. Obedience carries weight. Holiness carries weight. Broken repentance carries weight.
There is a reason Jesus repeatedly elevated invisible people while rebuking celebrated ones.
“And greetings in the markets, and to be called of men, Rabbi, Rabbi.”
But then Christ says something devastating.
“But he that is greatest among you shall be your servant.”
The word servant here comes from the Greek:
Not ruler. Not celebrity. Not elite spiritual aristocracy.
In the Kingdom of God, greatness descends before it rises.
That is why Jesus washed feet.
Imagine standing in a room where the Son of God wraps a towel around Himself while proud men argue about rank.
Even the apostle Paul — arguably one of the greatest theological minds in history — introduced himself repeatedly as:
Not celebrity preacher. Not global authority. Not spiritual superstar.
Modern culture teaches people to build names.
The Gospel teaches people to die.
“If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me.”
The phrase “deny himself” in Greek is:
It means to utterly disown oneself.
This is why genuine discipleship feels violent to pride.
Even in the Hebrew Scriptures, God constantly bypassed human systems of status.
And Jesus Himself was born in conditions the world would consider humiliating.
Isaiah prophesied this centuries before Christ came:
“He is despised and rejected of men.”
The Hebrew word for despised is:
The Savior entered the world without earthly prestige because God was exposing humanity’s blindness.
People still judge importance the same way they did in the days of Samuel.
By appearance. By stature. By image. By presentation.
“For the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.”
The Hebrew word for heart is:
It refers to the inner self:
God examines what public audiences cannot see.
Because many people build spiritual reputations while secretly rotting internally.
Jesus reserved some of His strongest language for religious performers.
“Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites!”
Christ was essentially calling religious leaders theatrical pretenders.
Men who mastered appearance while lacking transformation.
And honestly, very little has changed.
There are people with microphones who do not pray.
People teaching purity while addicted in secret.
People preaching surrender while worshipping money.
People building ministries while neglecting intimacy with God.
People chasing influence instead of holiness.
And heaven is not fooled by any of it.
“Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof.”
The phrase “form of godliness” comes from:
An outward shape without inward substance.
The frightening reality is that some people are more committed to protecting their image than confronting their sin.
But Scripture keeps exposing this illusion.
Ecclesiastes destroys human pride with brutal honesty.
But the word הֶבֶל (heḇel) literally means:
One illness. One funeral. One tragedy. One coffin.
“For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?”
Your life. Your inner being. Your eternal self.
What is the value of temporary success if your eternal condition is bankrupt?
This is where modern Christianity desperately needs repentance.
Too many believers are trying to look anointed instead of becoming holy.
Too many churches market personalities more than Christ.
Too many people know Christian language without knowing God.
And deep down, many are exhausted from pretending.
There is freedom in honesty before God.
David understood this after his sin.
“The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise.”
God can work with shattered honesty.
God literally positions Himself against the proud.
Imagine fighting God just to protect your ego.
The terrifying part is that pride can wear religious clothing.
In Isaiah 14, the repeated language is:
“I will ascend.” “I will exalt.” “I will be like the most High.”
But the Kingdom moves the opposite direction.
This is the heart of Christ.
“Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him.”
Heaven exalts what earth often ignores.
This is why some unknown grandmother praying faithfully in private may carry more eternal weight than a famous preacher with millions of views.
And when eternity arrives, titles will disappear.
Revelation describes elders casting crowns before the throne.
Even heavenly rewards become acts of surrender.
Because in the presence of God, human glory finally appears microscopic.
That is the future every believer is moving toward.
One day, every hidden motive will be exposed.
Every secret compromise. Every private act. Every concealed wound. Every false performance. Every surrendered sacrifice.
That should sober every soul reading this.
Especially those building identities around human recognition.
Because your title cannot save you.
The Gospel was never an invitation to become impressive.
It was an invitation to die and be remade.
And resurrection only comes after surrender.
Somebody reading this has spent years trying to appear spiritually strong while secretly collapsing inside.
And maybe this is the first time you realize God was never asking for performance.
Yet God restored broken people who stopped pretending.
But Scripture repeatedly warns that proud religious actors harden themselves beyond repentance.
That is why this matters so deeply.
Your title means nothing if your heart belongs nowhere near God.
And yet grace is still available.
That is the scandal of the Gospel.
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
For exhausted hypocrites ready to stop pretending.
For religious actors finally removing the mask.
For wounded souls desperate for mercy.
Because eternity is approaching faster than most people realize.
And when you stand before God, your title means nothing.
What will matter is whether you truly knew Christ… and whether Christ truly knew you.
If this exposed something you’ve been hiding, you already know why this was hard to read.
Somebody you love is silently fighting this.
Stay close if you’re serious about letting God change you.
